title: Longest Word Built One Letter at a Time
hints: a word is buildable exactly when there's an unbroken chain of complete words from length 1 up to its own length - which structure lets you check 'is this whole path made of complete words' without repeatedly re-scanning?
insert every word into a trie, marking end-of-word nodes as usual
do a traversal (DFS works well) starting at the root, but only step into a child if that child node is itself marked end-of-word - stepping into a non-word node would break the chain
track the best word found so far during the traversal: prefer longer length, and break ties by lexicographically smaller
visiting children in sorted (alphabetical) order during the DFS makes the tie-break easy, since the first longest word you find at maximum depth is automatically the smallest
commonMistakes: forgetting that length-1 words are always trivially buildable, since they need no shorter prefix
breaking ties by insertion order or by the largest word instead of lexicographically smallest
checking prefixes against the word itself (off-by-one) instead of strictly shorter prefixes

content.problemStatement:
You're given a space-delimited string of lowercase `words`. A word can be
"built one character at a time" if every one of its non-empty prefixes
(not counting the full word itself, but including single-character
prefixes) also appears somewhere in the list.

**Find the longest word in the list that can be built one character at a time, breaking ties by returning the lexicographically smallest one.**

A word of length 1 is always considered buildable, since it has no shorter
prefix to require. If no word can be built, return an empty string.
constraints: words[i] consists of lowercase English letters, words separated by single spaces
notes: no word in the list is buildable and there's no single-character word (answer is empty string)
a tie in length between two buildable words, resolved lexicographically
a single-character word present with no longer buildable word (that character is the answer)

sampleTestCases.explanation: every prefix of "world" ("w", "wo", "wor", "worl") is present in the list

sampleTestCases.input: words = "a banana app appl ap apply apple"
sampleTestCases.explanation: "apple" and "apply" are both fully buildable and tie at length 5; "apple" is lexicographically smaller
neither word is buildable ("ab" is missing for "abc", "b" and "bc" are missing for "bcd"), and there is no single-character word either

testCases.input: ["a banana app appl ap apply apple"]
["a b c ab bc ac abc"]
["p pa pal pale palet palett palette"]
["no words match at all here so"]

optimal.time: O(total characters) to build and traverse
optimal.pattern: insert all words into a trie, then run a DFS/BFS from the root that only continues through nodes marked as end-of-word, tracking the longest (then lexicographically smallest) word reached

bruteForce.approach: put all words in a set; for each word, check whether every one of its prefixes (of length 1 up to length-1) is also in the set, then track the best buildable word seen
bruteForce.time: O(n * m^2) where n is word count and m is max word length, due to substring creation per prefix check
